paragraphs: If we ask what precisely the greatest good of all consists in, which should be the aim of every system of legislation, we will find that it comes down to two main objects, liberty and equality: liberty, because every particular dependence takes that much force away from the body of the State, and equality, because liberty cannot exist without it.

I have already defined civil liberty. By equality we should understand not that the degrees of power and wealth are to be exactly the same for everybody, but that power should never be great enough for violence and should always be exercised by virtue of rank and law; and that, in respect of wealth, no citizen should ever be rich enough to buy another, and none poor enough to be forced to sell himself:[1] which implies, on the part of the great, moderation in goods and position, and, on the part of the common sort, moderation in greed and covetousness.

We are told that such equality is an impractical ideal that cannot actually exist. But if its abuse is inevitable, does it follow that we should not at least regulate it? It is precisely because the force of circumstances tends continually to destroy equality that the force of legislation should always tend to maintain it.

But these general aims of every good system of legislation need to be modified in each country according to its local situation and the temperament of its inhabitants; and these circumstances should determine, in each case, the particular system of institutions that is best, perhaps not in itself, but for the State it is meant for. If, for instance, the soil is barren and unproductive, or the country too crowded for its inhabitants, the people should turn to industry and the crafts, and exchange what they produce for the goods they lack. If, on the other hand, a people lives on rich plains and fertile slopes, or, in a good land, lacks inhabitants, it should give all its attention to agriculture, which makes people multiply, and should drive out the crafts, which would only depopulate the country by gathering the few inhabitants there are into a few places.[2] If a nation lives on an extensive and convenient coastline, let it cover the sea with ships and foster commerce and navigation. It will have a life that is short and glorious. If, on its coasts, the sea washes nothing but almost inaccessible rocks, let it remain barbarous and live on fish: it will have a quieter, perhaps a better, and certainly a happier life. In a word, besides the principles common to all, every nation has in itself something that gives them a particular application and makes its legislation its own. Thus among the Jews long ago, and more recently among the Arabs, the chief object was religion; among the Athenians, letters; at Carthage and Tyre, commerce; at Rhodes, shipping; at Sparta, war; at Rome, virtue. The author of _The Spirit of the Laws_ has shown, with many examples, by what art the legislator directs the constitution toward each of these objects.

What makes the constitution of a State truly solid and lasting is that what is fitting is carefully observed, so that natural relations and the laws always agree on every point, and law serves only, so to speak, to secure, accompany and correct them. But if the legislator mistakes his object and adopts a principle other than the one circumstances naturally point to — if his principle makes for servitude while they make for liberty, or if it makes for riches while they make for a large population, or if it makes for peace while they make for conquest — the laws will insensibly lose their influence, the constitution will change, and the State will have no rest from trouble until it is either destroyed or changed, and nature has resumed her invincible sway.
